title: The Language of Chemistry
tagline: Symbols, valency, radicals, formulae, balanced equations and relative atomic mass — the working vocabulary of every reaction in this course.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Chemistry syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Chemistry has its own alphabet. Symbols name the elements, formulae name the compounds, and equations describe how substances change. This chapter builds that alphabet step by step: you will learn the valencies of common elements and radicals, use them to write correct formulae, balance equations so that atoms are conserved, and calculate relative atomic and molecular masses. Every later chapter — chemical changes, water, bonding — assumes this vocabulary is secure, so accuracy here matters more than speed.

facts.label: Symbol rule
facts.value: One or two letters; first capital, second lower case (Ca is calcium, CO is carbon monoxide)

facts.label: Valency
facts.value: The combining capacity of an element or radical, written as a number or a sign (Na is +1, Cl is -1)

facts.label: Equation rule
facts.value: Atoms are neither created nor destroyed, so every element must balance on both sides

blocks.text: Every element is represented by a one- or two-letter symbol taken from its name. The first letter is always a capital and, when a second letter is present, it is lower case: Na is sodium, not SN or nA. A few symbols come from Latin names — Fe for iron (ferrum), Cu for copper (cuprum), Ag for silver (argentum) — and these simply have to be learned. A formula combines symbols to name a compound, and subscripts tell you how many atoms of each element are in one molecule or formula unit: H2O has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom, CO2 has one carbon and two oxygens, and CaCl2 has one calcium and two chlorines.

items.meaning: A one- or two-letter abbreviation for an element, such as O for oxygen or Fe for iron.
A combination of symbols showing the kinds and numbers of atoms in one unit of a substance, such as NH3 or CaCO3.
The small number written after a symbol that tells how many atoms of that element are present: the 4 in H2SO4 means four oxygen atoms.
The smallest particle of a covalent substance that still has the properties of that substance, such as O2 or CO2.

items: Write symbols with correct case: Mg is magnesium, MG and mg are wrong.
A subscript applies only to the symbol immediately before it: Ca(NO3)2 has two nitrogen atoms and six oxygen atoms.
Parentheses are used when a group of atoms repeats: Ca(OH)2 contains two hydroxide groups.
A number in front of a formula (a coefficient) multiplies the whole formula: 3H2O means three molecules of water.

items.text: Read Ca(NO3)2 aloud: one calcium, two nitrogen, six oxygen.
items.note: The bracket multiplies everything inside it: 2 x 1 nitrogen = 2 N, 2 x 3 oxygen = 6 O.

items.text: Count atoms in 2Al2(SO4)3: aluminium = 4, sulphur = 6, oxygen = 24.
items.note: Coefficient 2 multiplies the formula, then subscripts apply: 2 x 2 = 4 Al, 2 x 3 = 6 S, 2 x 3 x 4 = 24 O.

blocks.text: Valency is the combining capacity of an element — the number of bonds its atom forms, or equivalently the number of electrons it gains, loses or shares to reach a stable arrangement. Monovalent elements such as sodium, potassium and silver combine with one partner; divalent elements such as magnesium, calcium and oxygen combine with two; aluminium is trivalent. A radical is a group of atoms that behaves as a single unit with a fixed valency: nitrate NO3 is -1, sulphate SO4 is -2, carbonate CO3 is -2, hydroxide OH is -1 and ammonium NH4 is +1. Writing a formula is then a matter of balancing total positive valency against total negative valency so that the compound is electrically neutral.

items.meaning: The combining capacity of an element or radical; numerically it is the number of hydrogen atoms one atom of the element combines with or replaces.
A group of atoms that carries a valency and acts as a single unit in reactions, such as sulphate SO4 or ammonium NH4.
Valency shown by transfer of electrons, as in ionic compounds such as NaCl.
Valency shown by sharing of electrons, as in covalent compounds such as H2O and CH4.

items: Common positive valencies: Na +1, K +1, Ag +1, NH4 +1, Ca +2, Mg +2, Zn +2, Cu +2, Fe +2 or +3, Al +3.
Common negative valencies: Cl -1, OH -1, NO3 -1, MnO4 -1, O -2, S -2, CO3 -2, SO4 -2, PO4 -3.
To write a formula, write the metal (or positive radical) first, then the non-metal (or negative radical), and cross the valencies to give the simplest whole-number ratio.
The final formula must be the simplest ratio: MgO, never Mg2O2, because magnesium oxide exists in a 1:1 ratio.

items.text: Aluminium sulphate: Al has valency +3, SO4 has valency -2. Crossing gives Al2(SO4)3.
items.note: Check neutrality: 2 x (+3) = +6 and 3 x (-2) = -6. Total is zero, so the formula is correct.

items.text: Ammonium nitrate: NH4 is +1, NO3 is -1. The ratio is 1:1, so the formula is NH4NO3.
items.note: Both parts are radicals, but the same crossing rule applies.

items.text: Calcium hydroxide: Ca is +2, OH is -1, so Ca(OH)2 with the hydroxide in brackets.
items.note: Without brackets CaOH2 would suggest one calcium, one oxygen and two hydrogens — a different, wrong count.

blocks.text: A word equation names the reactants on the left and the products on the right. A chemical equation replaces those names with formulae, and a balanced equation has equal numbers of atoms of each element on both sides. Balancing follows the law of conservation of mass: atoms are only rearranged, never created or destroyed. Start by balancing each element in turn, leave hydrogen and oxygen until last, and finish by checking every atom. If a fractional coefficient appears, multiply the whole equation through to remove it.

items: Write the correct formulae first — balancing cannot fix a wrong formula.
List the count of atoms of each element on both sides before changing anything.
Balance metals first, then non-metals, then hydrogen and oxygen.
Never change a subscript to balance; only change coefficients.
Add state symbols where asked: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) aqueous.

items.text: Iron + steam -> iron(II,III) oxide + hydrogen. Balanced: 3Fe + 4H2O -> Fe3O4 + 4H2.
items.note: Fe: 3 = 3; H: 8 = 8; O: 4 = 4. The check on all three elements is what proves the equation balanced.

items.text: Aluminium + hydrochloric acid -> aluminium chloride + hydrogen. Balanced: 2Al + 6HCl -> 2AlCl3 + 3H2.

items.note: Carbon balances first, then hydrogen, then oxygen by adjusting the O2 coefficient.

blocks.text: Some reactions are easier to balance by inspection of half-equations. Oxidation and reduction, for example, can be checked by counting electrons transferred: if iron loses electrons and copper gains the same number, the equation is balanced for charge as well as for atoms. In this course, atom counting is sufficient, but the habit of checking every element separately is the habit that prevents lost marks.

Relative atomic mass (Ar) compares an atom's mass with one twelfth the mass of a carbon-12 atom; it has no unit because it is a ratio. Relative molecular mass (Mr) is the sum of the Ar values of all atoms in a molecule or formula unit — it is simply addition. For example, water H2O has Mr = (2 x 1) + 16 = 18, and calcium carbonate CaCO3 has Mr = 40 + 12 + (3 x 16) = 100. Percent composition by mass follows from the same numbers: divide the mass contributed by the element in one formula unit by the Mr of the compound and multiply by 100.

items.text: Mr of sulphuric acid H2SO4 = (2 x 1) + 32 + (4 x 16) = 98.
items.note: Add in the order the atoms appear; keep a running total to avoid arithmetic slips.

items.text: Percentage of nitrogen in ammonium nitrate NH4NO3: Mr = 14 + 4 + 14 + 48 = 80, so nitrogen = (28/80) x 100 = 35 per cent.
items.note: Two nitrogen atoms contribute 28, not 14 — count every atom in the formula.

items.text: Ar of chlorine from CaCl2: 111 - 40 = 71 for two chlorines, so Ar = 71/2 = 35.5.
items.note: Relative atomic masses are often non-integers because they are weighted averages of isotopes.

items.meaning: The weighted average mass of one atom of an element compared with one twelfth the mass of a carbon-12 atom; has no units.
The sum of the relative atomic masses of all atoms in one molecule or formula unit.
Mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction, so the total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products.
A pure compound always contains the same elements in the same proportion by mass, whatever its source or method of preparation.

figures.caption: Figure: Writing a formula by crossing valencies
figures.description: Aluminium (valency +3) written above sulphate SO4 (valency -2); crossing the valency numbers gives Al2(SO4)3, and the check 2 x (+3) + 3 x (-2) = 0 confirms neutrality.

figures.caption: Figure: Atom-count check for a balanced equation
figures.description: For 3Fe + 4H2O -> Fe3O4 + 4H2, tally the atoms of each element in two columns (left and right) — Fe 3/3, H 8/8, O 4/4 — and confirm every row matches before accepting the equation.

keyPoints: Symbols start with a capital letter; a second letter, if present, is lower case (Ca, Fe, Na).
A subscript counts only the atoms of the symbol or bracket immediately before it.
Valency is combining capacity; radicals are groups of atoms with fixed valency.
To write a formula, cross the valencies and simplify to the smallest whole-number ratio.
A balanced equation has equal numbers of atoms of every element on both sides.
Balance by changing coefficients only — never change subscripts to balance an equation.
Relative atomic mass (Ar) has no units; relative molecular mass (Mr) is the sum of Ar values.
The law of conservation of mass requires equal total mass of reactants and products.
The law of constant proportions: a compound always has the same elements in the same mass ratio.
examFocus: Formula questions reward the neutrality check — always show that total positive valency equals total negative valency.
In balancing questions, write the atom tally for both sides; examiners look for the check, not just the final coefficients.
Percent composition needs three steps: Mr of the compound, total mass of the element in question, then the percentage — skipping the middle step loses method marks.
Watch for hydrates and brackets: Ca(OH)2 and CuSO4.5H2O both test whether you multiply through parentheses correctly.

vocabulary.meaning: Combining capacity of an element or radical.
A group of atoms acting as a single unit with fixed valency, e.g. NO3 (nitrate).
One- or two-letter abbreviation of an element, e.g. Fe for iron.
Symbols and subscripts naming one unit of a compound, e.g. CaCO3.
Number in front of a formula showing how many formula units take part.
Sum of the relative atomic masses of all atoms in a molecule.

questions.prompt: Which symbol is correct for calcium?
questions.explanation: The first letter of a symbol is capitalised and any second letter is lower case, so calcium is Ca.
questions.commonMistake: Writing CA in a hurry; capital letters on both letters denote a different, incorrect symbol.

questions.prompt: The formula of aluminium sulphate is:
questions.explanation: Aluminium has valency +3 and sulphate has valency -2; crossing the valencies gives Al2(SO4)3, which is electrically neutral.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing AlSO4, which would leave unequal total valencies (+3 against -2).

questions.prompt: How many oxygen atoms are present in one formula unit of Ca(NO3)2?
questions.explanation: The bracket multiplies everything inside it: 2 x 3 oxygen atoms = 6 oxygen atoms, plus one calcium and 2 nitrogen atoms.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 3 by ignoring the coefficient of 2 outside the bracket.

questions.explanation: Counting each element gives Al 2 = 2, S 3 = 3, H 6 = 6 and O 12 = 12, so only the first option balances.
questions.commonMistake: Balancing sulphur but forgetting to re-check hydrogen and oxygen afterwards.

questions.prompt: The relative molecular mass of CaCO3 is (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16):
questions.commonMistake: Adding only one oxygen atom, which gives 68.

questions.prompt: Which is a radical with a valency of -2?
questions.explanation: Sulphate carries a charge of 2- and therefore has valency 2. Nitrate and hydroxide are -1, and ammonium is +1.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing ammonium (+1) with the negative radicals because it is written as a group.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the group of atoms SO4 is called ________ and has a valency of ________.
questions.explanation: SO4 is the sulphate radical. Its charge is 2-, so in formula writing it combines with two monovalent partners or one divalent partner.
questions.commonMistake: Calling it sulphite, which is SO3.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in the reaction 3Fe + 4H2O -> Fe3O4 + 4H2, the number of hydrogen atoms on each side is ________.
questions.explanation: Four water molecules give 4 x 2 = 8 hydrogen atoms on the left, and four hydrogen molecules give 4 x 2 = 8 on the right.
questions.commonMistake: Counting the coefficient 4 as the number of hydrogen atoms instead of multiplying by the subscript 2.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the relative atomic mass has ________ unit(s) because it is a ________.
questions.answer: no; ratio (comparison with one twelfth the mass of a carbon-12 atom)
questions.explanation: Relative atomic mass compares masses, so it is a pure number with no physical unit.
questions.commonMistake: Writing 'grams' or 'amu' — relative masses are dimensionless.

questions.prompt: Write the formulae of (a) calcium chloride (b) sodium sulphate (c) ammonium carbonate.
questions.answer: (a) CaCl2 — Ca is +2 and Cl is -1, so two chlorines. (b) Na2SO4 — Na is +1 and SO4 is -2, so two sodiums. (c) (NH4)2CO3 — NH4 is +1 and CO3 is -2, so two ammonium groups in brackets.
questions.explanation: In each case the total positive valency must equal the total negative valency, and repeating radicals must be enclosed in brackets.
questions.commonMistake: Writing NaSO4 or NH4CO3 by forgetting to balance the positive side against the -2 radical.

questions.prompt: Balance the equation: Al + HCl -> AlCl3 + H2.
questions.explanation: Aluminium needs a coefficient of 2 to balance the 2 Al in Al2Cl6 terms; then 6 HCl provides 6 chlorine atoms for 2 AlCl3 and 6 hydrogen atoms for 3 H2.
questions.commonMistake: Writing Al + 3HCl -> AlCl3 + 1.5H2 — fractional coefficients must be cleared by multiplying the whole equation by 2.

questions.prompt: Calculate the relative molecular mass of (a) H2SO4 (b) Al2(SO4)3. (H = 1, S = 32, O = 16, Al = 27)
questions.explanation: Sum the atomic masses of every atom in the formula; in part (b) the sulphate group contributes 96 and appears three times.
questions.commonMistake: Using 64 for the whole SO4 group without multiplying by 3 in part (b).

questions.prompt: State the two laws that chemical equations must satisfy and explain how each is reflected in a balanced equation.
questions.answer: The law of conservation of mass: atoms are not created or destroyed, so each element must appear in equal numbers on both sides — this is exactly what balancing achieves. The law of constant proportions: a compound always contains its elements in fixed mass ratios, so formulas never change subscripts during balancing; only coefficients change.
questions.explanation: Balancing adjusts coefficients to conserve atoms, while the fixed subscripts inside formulas preserve the compound's constant composition.
questions.commonMistake: Changing a subscript to make the counts match, which alters the compound itself and breaks the law of constant proportions.

questions.prompt: Write and balance the equation for the reaction of sodium carbonate with dilute hydrochloric acid to produce sodium chloride, water and carbon dioxide. State what you would observe.
questions.answer: Na2CO3 + 2HCl -> 2NaCl + H2O + CO2. Balanced check: Na 2 = 2, C 1 = 1, O 3 = 1 + 2 = 3, H 2 = 2, Cl 2 = 2. Observation: effervescence — brisk effervescence of carbon dioxide gas, which turns lime water milky.
questions.explanation: Carbonate plus acid gives a salt, water and carbon dioxide. The two NaCl units are needed because sodium carbonate contains two sodium atoms, and each sodium needs one chlorine from HCl.
questions.commonMistake: Writing Na2CO3 + HCl -> NaCl + H2O + CO2 and stopping before the equation balances for sodium, chlorine and hydrogen.

questions.prompt: A compound contains 40 per cent carbon, 6.7 per cent hydrogen and 53.3 per cent oxygen by mass. Its relative molecular mass is 180. Find its empirical formula and molecular formula. (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
questions.answer: Divide each percentage by the atomic mass: C 40/12 = 3.33, H 6.7/1 = 6.7, O 53.3/16 = 3.33. Divide by the smallest (3.33): C 1, H 2, O 1, so the empirical formula is CH2O with a formula mass of 30. The molecular formula is 180/30 = 6 times the empirical formula, so C6H12O6.
questions.explanation: Percentages are converted to relative moles by dividing by atomic masses, then simplified to the smallest whole-number ratio; the molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula.
questions.commonMistake: Stopping at the empirical formula, or dividing by the smallest number before checking that the ratios are near-whole numbers.

questions.prompt: Why is it wrong to balance an equation by changing the subscript in H2O to H2O2?
questions.answer: Changing the subscript creates a different substance — hydrogen peroxide instead of water — so the equation no longer describes the actual reaction. Balancing may only change the number of formula units (coefficients), because atoms are rearranged but the identity of each compound is fixed by its constant composition.
questions.explanation: Subscripts define the compound's composition (law of constant proportions); coefficients describe how many units react. Only coefficients may vary during balancing.
questions.commonMistake: Treating formulas as adjustable quantities rather than fixed names for substances.
